## What the package does

`TriCopula` estimates a joint regression model for three continuous
responses. Each response has its own distribution and its own regression
equations, and a trivariate copula links the three:

$$
\log f(y_1, y_2, y_3 \mid x) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} \log f_j(y_j \mid x)
  + \log c\{F_1(y_1 \mid x), F_2(y_2 \mid x), F_3(y_3 \mid x)\}.
$$

All parameters, of the margins and of the copula, are estimated together by
maximum likelihood, so that one covariance matrix covers everything.

| Component | Options |
|---|---|
| Margins | `gaussian`, `lognormal`, `gamma`, `weibull`, `invgauss`, `beta`, `gpareto`, `dagum`, `singhmaddala` |
| Mean / location | linear predictor in each margin |
| Scale / shape | linear predictor in each margin (`scale`) |
| Third parameter | Dagum and Singh-Maddala margins: linear predictor (`shape`) |
| Copula | trivariate `gaussian`, `student`, or pair-copula construction `pcc` |
| Dependence | linear predictor for each dependence parameter (`dependence`) |
| Degrees of freedom | constant, or a linear predictor (`df`) |
| Vine root | first response, or `root = 2`, `3`; `tc_select(root = "auto")` |
| Simplifying assumption | simplified vine, or `simplified = FALSE` (the conditional pair depends on the level of the root) |
| Incomplete observation | `truncation` (known bounds per response), `censoring` (right, left, interval), missing responses |

This is a research prototype. The related package **GJRM** offers
`gjrm.pcc()`, which takes three fitted margins as given and then estimates a
pair-copula construction step by step, with many more distributions, smooth
terms and automatic family selection. `TriCopula` is narrower but estimates
everything jointly. The two were checked against each other during
development: on common models they evaluate the same likelihood.

## Data: Spanish manufacturing firms

The illustration uses the 1990 cross-section of the Spanish firm panel
`Snmesp` shipped with the **plm** package (738 firms; Alonso-Borrego and
Arellano, 1999). The three outcomes are output, employment and the average
wage; the covariate is the capital stock (in logs, centred). The analysis is
descriptive: it shows how the three outcomes vary jointly with capital, not
a causal effect of capital.

```{r data}
library(TriCopula)
data("Snmesp", package = "plm")
firms <- subset(Snmesp, year == 1990)
firms$output     <- exp(firms$y)
firms$employment <- exp(firms$n)
firms$wage       <- exp(firms$w)
firms$capital    <- firms$k - mean(firms$k)
summary(firms[c("output", "employment", "wage", "capital")])
forms <- list(output ~ capital, employment ~ capital, wage ~ capital)
```

## Step 1: margins

A fit is specified by three formulas and three margin names. Here every
outcome is positive and right-skewed, so log-normal and Gamma margins are
natural candidates; `tc_compare()` ranks alternatives by AIC and BIC.

```{r margins}
m_ln  <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = c("lognormal", "lognormal", "lognormal"))
m_mix <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = c("lognormal", "gamma", "gamma"))
m_ga  <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = c("gamma", "gamma", "gamma"))
tc_compare(m_ln, m_mix, m_ga)
mar <- c("lognormal", "lognormal", "lognormal")
```

The log-normal margins have the lowest AIC and are kept.

## Step 2: copula

The Gaussian copula has no tail dependence, the Student-t copula has
symmetric tail dependence, and a pair-copula construction (PCC) allows a
different family for each pair, including the asymmetric Clayton and Gumbel
families. `tc_select()` picks the three PCC families sequentially and then
fits the selected PCC jointly.

```{r copula}
fit_g <- m_ln
fit_t <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "student")
sel   <- tc_select(forms, firms, margins = mar)
sel$families
subset(sel$table, selected)
tc_compare(fit_g, fit_t, sel$fit)
```

Both heavier-tailed alternatives improve on the Gaussian copula. The
trivariate Student-t copula is the more parsimonious of the two and is used
below; the selected PCC tells the same story about the signs and sizes of
the dependence.

## Step 3: letting scale and dependence vary with capital

`scale` adds a regression for the log standard deviation of each margin and
`dependence` one for each dependence parameter. Nested models are compared
with a likelihood-ratio test.

```{r extend}
fit_s <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "student",
                   scale = ~ capital)
fit_d <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "student",
                   scale = ~ capital, dependence = ~ capital)
tc_lrtest(fit_t, fit_s)
tc_lrtest(fit_s, fit_d)
tc_compare(fit_t, fit_s, fit_d)
fit <- fit_d
```

## Results

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The coefficient table is on the estimation scale (logs for scales, `atanh`
for correlations). `tc_dependence()` gives the scale and dependence
parameters on their natural scale, averaged over the sample, and
`predict(type = "dependence")` shows how the dependence changes with
capital.

```{r dependence}
round(tc_dependence(fit), 3)
caps <- data.frame(capital = c(-2, 0, 2))
cbind(caps, round(predict(fit, caps, type = "dependence"), 3))
round(tc_taildep(fit), 3)
```

Reading the table (all correlations are between the outcomes at a given
level of capital):

- Output and employment are strongly positively dependent (`rho12`), and
  output and wages moderately so (`rho13`).
- `rho23|1` is the partial correlation between employment and wages given
  output. It is clearly negative: among firms with the same capital and the
  same output, those that employ more people pay lower average wages, which
  is what lower labour productivity would produce. The correlation without
  conditioning on output (`rho23`) is also negative but much weaker, because
  both employment and wages rise with output.
- The dependence between output and wages weakens as capital grows (second
  table), which is the main reason the model with covariate-dependent
  dependence is preferred.
- The estimated degrees of freedom imply only weak tail dependence.

### Marginal effects

`tc_effects()` reports the average effect of a covariate on the three
conditional means, allowing for its effect through the scale equations.

```{r effects}
tc_effects(fit, "capital")
```

### Joint probabilities

The fitted joint distribution gives probabilities of joint events. Here: the
probability that a firm is below the sample median on all three outcomes at
once, for three levels of capital, compared with what independence between
the outcomes would give.

```{r jointprob}
med <- sapply(firms[c("output", "employment", "wage")], median)
joint <- tc_jointprob(fit, med, caps)
pr <- predict(fit, caps)
indep <- plnorm(med[1], pr$margin1$meanlog, pr$margin1$sdlog) *
  plnorm(med[2], pr$margin2$meanlog, pr$margin2$sdlog) *
  plnorm(med[3], pr$margin3$meanlog, pr$margin3$sdlog)
cbind(caps, joint = round(joint, 3), if_independent = round(indep, 3))
```

## Checking the fit

`tc_diagnostics()` collects the optimizer checks (convergence, gradient,
information matrix), the gain of joint estimation over the two-stage
estimator, and simple specification checks on the probability integral
transforms.

```{r diagnostics}
tc_diagnostics(fit)
```

```{r pit, fig.cap = "Probability integral transforms of the three margins (uniform if the margins fit)."}
u <- tc_pit(fit)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (j in 1:3) hist(u[[j]], breaks = 15, main = c("output", "employment", "wage")[j],
                    xlab = "PIT", col = "grey85", border = "white")
par(op)
```

Two further checks are cheap and worth making routinely.

**Sandwich standard errors.** If the copula family is wrong, model-based
standard errors can be too small; sandwich standard errors remain valid.
Large differences between the two are a warning sign.

```{r sandwich}
se <- cbind(model = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))),
            sandwich = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, type = "sandwich"))))
round(cbind(se, ratio = se[, 2] / se[, 1]), 3)
```

**Joint versus two-stage estimates.** `fit$ifm` holds the two-stage
estimates (margins first, copula second). Under a correct model the two
agree up to sampling noise; a systematic shift in the marginal intercepts
points to a misspecified copula.

```{r ifm}
round(cbind(two_stage = fit$ifm$coefficients, joint = coef(fit),
            difference_in_se = (coef(fit) - fit$ifm$coefficients) /
              sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))), 3)[1:12, ]
```

## Other tools

```{r other, eval = FALSE}
# bootstrap standard errors and percentile intervals (parametric or by rows)
bt <- tc_bootstrap(fit, B = 200, type = "nonparametric")

# simulate new responses for given covariates
sim <- simulate(fit, newdata = caps, seed = 1)

# a pair-copula construction with chosen families
tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "pcc",
          families = c("student", "gumbel", "gaussian"))

# Frank and Joe pairs, the second response as root of the vine
tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "pcc",
          families = c("frank", "joe", "gaussian"), root = 2)

# degrees of freedom that depend on a covariate
tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "student", df = ~ capital)

# families and root chosen by AIC (three joint fits)
tc_select(forms, firms, margins = mar, candidates = "all", root = "auto")$roots

# a penalized smooth of capital in the first mean and in one dependence parameter
fs <- tricopula(list(output ~ s(capital), employment ~ capital, wage ~ capital),
                firms, margins = mar, dependence = list(~ s(capital), ~ 1, ~ 1))
summary(fs)$smooths
plot(fit ~ capital, tc_smooth(fs, 1), type = "l")
# intervals that allow for the uncertainty of the smoothing parameters
tc_smooth(fs, 1, type = "corrected")

# prior weights; rows with one or two missing responses kept. Weights that
# are not whole numbers count as sampling weights: sandwich standard errors
# tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, weights = w, missing = "likelihood")

# inference that allows for the selection of the families
# tc_bootstrap(sel$fit, B = 200, type = "nonparametric", select = TRUE)
# tc_select(forms, firms, margins = mar, split = 0.5, seed = 1)$fit
# the margins, the terms of the mean formulas and the copula type can be
# selected too; the bootstrap then also reports tail dependence and means
# tc_select(forms, firms, margins = list("lognormal", c("lognormal", "gamma"), "lognormal"),
#           covariates = "backward", copula = "auto")

# a non-simplified vine: the dependence of the conditional pair varies with
# the level of the first response; test of the simplifying assumption
# ns <- tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar, copula = "pcc",
#                 families = sel$families, simplified = FALSE)
# tc_smooth(ns, 1); tc_simplifying_test(sel$fit)

# censored and truncated responses: `status` is 1 for an exact value, 0 for
# a right-censored one; only firms with output above `a` are in the sample
# tricopula(forms, firms, margins = mar,
#           censoring = list(NULL, c(status = "status"), NULL),
#           truncation = list(c(a, Inf), NULL, NULL), truncation_type = "joint")

# three-parameter margins for heavy-tailed positive responses
tricopula(forms, firms, margins = c("dagum", "singhmaddala", "lognormal"),
          shape = list(~ capital, ~ 1, ~ 1))

# other margins, e.g. a share in (0, 1)
# tricopula(list(share ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x), d, margins = c("beta", "gamma", "weibull"))
```

## Limits to keep in mind

- Intervals and tests for smooth terms are approximate.
- A predictor for the Student-t degrees of freedom (`df`) needs a large
  sample to be estimated with any precision.
- In a PCC the families and the root are chosen by the user or by
  `tc_select()`; the standard errors of that fit do not account for the
  selection. `tc_select(split = )` and `tc_bootstrap(select = TRUE)` do.
- Joint estimation is more efficient than two-stage estimation when the
  model is right, and can be biased when the copula is wrong, most visibly
  under strong asymmetric tail dependence fitted with a symmetric copula.
- Censoring and truncation are available since 0.16.0; rows with several
  censored responses are slow. One censored response per row is integrated
  in closed form (default since 0.17.1); every fit reports the accuracy of its quadrature in
  `fit$cens_accuracy`. Missing responses are handled under the
  assumption that they are missing at random (`missing = "likelihood"`).

## Reference

Alonso-Borrego, C. and Arellano, M. (1999). Symmetrically normalized
instrumental-variable estimation using panel data. *Journal of Business and
Economic Statistics*, 17(1), 36-49.
